items.stem: Which hormone raises blood glucose?
items.answer: glucagon
items.markingKey: A. Stimulates glycogenolysis.

items.stem: Explain the difference between type 1 diabetes and type 2 diabetes.
items.answer: Type 1 diabetes is caused by autoimmune destruction of β cells so insulin is not produced, usually starting in childhood; type 2 diabetes is caused by insulin resistance, is linked to lifestyle and usually develops in adults.
items.markingKey: Type 1 diabetes is caused by autoimmune destruction of β cells so insulin is not produced, usually starting in childhood; type 2 diabetes is caused by insulin resistance, is linked to lifestyle and usually develops in adults. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Why is control of blood glucose an example of negative feedback?
options: Insulin and glucagon act in the same direction.
A rise or fall in glucose triggers hormone secretion that returns glucose to the set point.
items.answer: A rise or fall in glucose triggers hormone secretion that returns glucose to the set point.
items.markingKey: C. Reversal of change.

items.stem: During a 2-hour run, the glycogen content of a runner’s liver fell from 84 g to 28 g. Calculate the percentage change.
items.markingKey: (final − initial)/initial × 100 = (28 − 84)/84 × 100 (M1) = -66.7 % (A1); sign/direction required.

items.stem:
A glucose tolerance test was carried out: after fasting, each person drank 75 g of glucose and blood glucose was measured at intervals.

Time / min | Person A / mmol dm⁻³ | Person B / mmol dm⁻³
0 | 4.9 | 8.1
30 | 7.4 | 12.8
60 | 6.3 | 15.0
90 | 5.7 | 14.0
120 | 5.1 | 12.5
150 | 4.8 | 10.8

(a) State the maximum blood glucose of person B. [1]
(b) Calculate the mean rate of decrease in blood glucose of person A between 30 and 120 minutes. [2]
(c) Calculate the percentage increase in blood glucose of person B from 0 minutes to the maximum. [2]
items.answer: (a) 15.0 mmol dm⁻³ (b) 0.026 mmol dm⁻³ min⁻¹ (c) +85.2 %

items.stem: "Negative feedback means the response is harmful." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Negative feedback means the response reverses the change, restoring the set point.
items.markingKey: Negative feedback means the response reverses the change, restoring the set point. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Type 2 diabetes is caused entirely by lifestyle choices."
items.answer: Lifestyle is a major factor, but genetic and social factors also contribute, so it is not entirely a matter of individual choice.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: obesity, high-sugar diets and inactivity strongly increase risk; lifestyle change can reverse early type 2 diabetes. Arguments against: genetic factors and ethnicity affect risk; socio-economic factors limit access to healthy food and exercise. Supported judgement: Lifestyle is a major factor, but genetic and social factors also contribute, so it is not entirely a matter of individual choice.

items.stem: Explain how blood glucose concentration is regulated by negative feedback, and the causes and treatment of diabetes.
items.answer: Set point ~5 mmol dm⁻³; islets of Langerhans α and β cells; insulin: GLUT4, glycogenesis, respiration, fat storage; glucagon: glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis; negative feedback; type 1 autoimmune; type 2 resistance; treatments; glucose tolerance test.
items.markingKey: Set point ~5 mmol dm⁻³; islets of Langerhans α and β cells; insulin: GLUT4, glycogenesis, respiration, fat storage; glucagon: glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis; negative feedback; type 1 autoimmune; type 2 resistance; treatments; glucose tolerance test.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "type 2 diabetes".
items.answer: A condition in which target cells become resistant to insulin, often linked to obesity and inactivity
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a condition in which target cells become resistant to insulin, often linked to obesity and inactivity. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A control mechanism in which a change from the set point triggers responses that reverse the change"?
items.answer: negative feedback
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of negative feedback.

items.stem: Explain how blood glucose concentration is controlled.
items.answer: Glucose is monitored by cells of the pancreatic islets; when high, β cells secrete insulin, which causes uptake of glucose by liver, muscle and fat cells (GLUT4) and conversion to glycogen (glycogenesis); when low, α cells secrete glucagon, which stimulates glycogen breakdown (glycogenolysis) in the liver, releasing glucose; negative feedback returns glucose to the set point.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Glucose is monitored by cells of the pancreatic islets; when high, β cells secrete insulin, which causes uptake of glucose by liver, muscle and fat cells (GLUT4) and conversion to glycogen (glycogenesis); when low, α cells secrete glucagon, which stimulates glycogen breakdown (glycogenolysis) in the liver, releasing glucose; negative feedback returns glucose to the set point. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Why are both insulin and glucagon needed?
options: They act antagonistically, allowing correction of both rises and falls in blood glucose.
items.answer: They act antagonistically, allowing correction of both rises and falls in blood glucose.
items.markingKey: C. Antagonistic hormones.

items.stem: Distinguish between insulin and glucagon.
items.answer: Insulin is secreted by β cells when glucose is high and lowers blood glucose by increasing uptake and glycogen synthesis; glucagon is secreted by α cells when glucose is low and raises blood glucose by stimulating glycogen breakdown.
items.markingKey: Insulin is secreted by β cells when glucose is high and lowers blood glucose by increasing uptake and glycogen synthesis; glucagon is secreted by α cells when glucose is low and raises blood glucose by stimulating glycogen breakdown. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Glucagon and glycogen are the same thing." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Glucagon is a hormone; glycogen is a storage polysaccharide.
items.markingKey: Glucagon is a hormone; glycogen is a storage polysaccharide. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to the rise in type 2 diabetes worldwide, explain how it illustrates insulin resistance.
items.answer: Over 500 million adults have diabetes, most with type 2, linked to obesity and sedentary lifestyles. Excess fat and inactivity reduce the response of target cells to insulin, so blood glucose remains high.
items.markingKey: Context (Over 500 million adults have diabetes, most with type 2, linked to obesity and sedentary lifestyles.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Excess fat and inactivity reduce the response of target cells to insulin, so blood glucose remains high. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to insulin resistance.

items.stem: An athlete runs a long race and blood glucose begins to fall. Which response is expected?
options: Glucagon secretion increases and the liver breaks down glycogen.
items.answer: Glucagon secretion increases and the liver breaks down glycogen.
items.markingKey: A. Restore glucose.

items.stem: In an untreated person with type 1 diabetes, which is expected after a meal?
options: Blood glucose rises and stays high because no insulin is secreted.
items.answer: Blood glucose rises and stays high because no insulin is secreted.
items.markingKey: B. No insulin.

items.stem: Using the discovery of insulin by Banting and Best (1921) as an example, explain hormonal control of blood glucose.
items.answer: Extracts of dog pancreas lowered blood glucose in diabetic dogs; in 1922 insulin saved the life of Leonard Thompson. Insulin from β cells is required to lower blood glucose, so replacing it treats type 1 diabetes.
items.markingKey: Context (Extracts of dog pancreas lowered blood glucose in diabetic dogs; in 1922 insulin saved the life of Leonard Thompson.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Insulin from β cells is required to lower blood glucose, so replacing it treats type 1 diabetes. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to hormonal control of blood glucose.

items.stem: Describe the principles of homeostasis using examples.
items.answer: Internal environment; set point; receptors, control centre, effectors; negative feedback; examples: blood glucose, body temperature, water balance; positive feedback contrasts (childbirth, LH surge).
items.markingKey: Internal environment; set point; receptors, control centre, effectors; negative feedback; examples: blood glucose, body temperature, water balance; positive feedback contrasts (childbirth, LH surge).

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "brown adipose tissue".
items.answer: Fat tissue with many mitochondria that generates heat by uncoupled respiration (thermogenesis)
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: fat tissue with many mitochondria that generates heat by uncoupled respiration (thermogenesis). Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between vasodilation and vasoconstriction.
items.answer: Vasodilation widens skin arterioles, increasing blood flow to the surface and heat loss; vasoconstriction narrows them, reducing blood flow and conserving heat.
items.markingKey: Vasodilation widens skin arterioles, increasing blood flow to the surface and heat loss; vasoconstriction narrows them, reducing blood flow and conserving heat. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Sweat cools you because it is cold." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Cooling is due to evaporation, which absorbs heat from the skin.
items.markingKey: Cooling is due to evaporation, which absorbs heat from the skin. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:

Time / min | Core temperature / °C | Skin temperature / °C | Sweat rate / g h⁻¹
0 | 37.0 | 32.6 | 6
5 | 37.3 | 33.0 | 32
10 | 37.7 | 34.0 | 115

20 | 38.1 | 34.6 | 360
25 | 38.1 | 34.6 | 396
30 | 38.0 | 34.7 | 302

(a) State the maximum core temperature. [1]
(b) Calculate the heat lost per hour by evaporation at the final sweat rate (2.4 kJ g⁻¹), assuming all sweat evaporates. [1]
A person enters a cold room. Which combination of responses is expected?
items.answer: vasoconstriction, shivering and increased thyroxine
items.markingKey: D. Reduce heat loss, increase production.

items.stem: Explain the importance of maintaining a constant core temperature.
items.answer: Enzymes have optimum temperatures; too high: denaturation; too low: slow reactions; nervous function; consequences of hypothermia and hyperthermia; heat stroke.
items.markingKey: Enzymes have optimum temperatures; too high: denaturation; too low: slow reactions; nervous function; consequences of hypothermia and hyperthermia; heat stroke.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "thyroxine"?
options: A hormone secreted by α cells of the pancreatic islets when blood glucose is low, which stimulates glycogen breakdown in the liver
Cells of Bowman’s capsule with foot-like extensions that leave filtration slits
A hormone from the thyroid gland that increases metabolic rate and heat production
The reabsorption of useful substances such as glucose, amino acids and much of the water and ions from the filtrate back into the blood, mainly in the proximal convoluted tubule
items.answer: A hormone from the thyroid gland that increases metabolic rate and heat production
items.markingKey: C. "thyroxine" is a hormone from the thyroid gland that increases metabolic rate and heat production.

items.stem: Which part of the brain acts as the thermoregulatory centre?
items.answer: the hypothalamus
items.markingKey: A. Monitors blood temperature.

items.stem: Why does vasodilation increase heat loss?
options: More blood flows through capillaries near the skin surface, so more heat is lost by radiation and convection.
Blood vessels move to the surface.
items.answer: More blood flows through capillaries near the skin surface, so more heat is lost by radiation and convection.
items.markingKey: C. Arterioles dilate.

items.stem: Why do small mammals have higher metabolic rates per gram than large ones?
options: They do not need to stay warm.
Their large surface area to volume ratio causes faster heat loss.
items.answer: Their large surface area to volume ratio causes faster heat loss.
items.markingKey: C. SA:V.

items.stem: Which response reduces heat loss in a cold environment?
items.answer: vasoconstriction of skin arterioles
items.markingKey: C. Less blood near surface.

items.stem: A hiker in hot weather lost 0.85 kg of sweat during exercise, of which 80 % evaporated from the skin. Evaporation of 1 g of water removes 2.4 kJ. Calculate the heat removed by evaporation.
With reference to brown fat in newborn babies, explain how it illustrates non-shivering thermogenesis.
items.answer: Newborns have deposits of brown adipose tissue between the shoulder blades. Uncoupled respiration in brown fat releases heat instead of making ATP, helping babies stay warm.
items.markingKey: Context (Newborns have deposits of brown adipose tissue between the shoulder blades.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Uncoupled respiration in brown fat releases heat instead of making ATP, helping babies stay warm. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to non-shivering thermogenesis.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Endothermy is a better strategy than ectothermy."
items.answer: Endothermy gives independence from environmental temperature at a high energy cost; which is better depends on habitat and food supply.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: endotherms can remain active in cold conditions and at night; enzymes work at a constant optimum. Arguments against: endotherms need much more food energy; ectotherms survive on less food and in deserts can be very successful. Supported judgement: Endothermy gives independence from environmental temperature at a high energy cost; which is better depends on habitat and food supply.

items.stem:
A student exercised on a cycle ergometer for 30 minutes in a warm room. Core (rectal) temperature, skin temperature and sweat rate were recorded.

Time / min | Core temperature / °C | Skin temperature / °C | Sweat rate / g h⁻¹
0 | 37.0 | 32.4 | 5
5 | 37.3 | 33.1 | 26
10 | 37.7 | 33.9 | 135
15 | 38.0 | 34.4 | 270
20 | 38.1 | 34.5 | 375
25 | 38.1 | 34.5 | 322
30 | 38.0 | 34.4 | 322

(a) State the maximum core temperature. [1]
(b) Calculate the heat lost per hour by evaporation at the final sweat rate (2.4 kJ g⁻¹), assuming all sweat evaporates. [1]
(c) Describe the changes in core temperature and sweat rate. [2]
(d) Explain why core temperature rises at the start of exercise. [2]
items.answer: (a) 38.1 °C (b) 773 kJ h⁻¹ (c) Core temperature rises during the first 15–20 min then levels off; sweat rate rises sharply after a delay and then plateaus. (d) Muscle contraction increases respiration, which releases heat faster than it is lost.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 38.1 (A1). (b) [1] 322 × 2.4 = 773 (A1). (c) [2] Core rise then plateau (A1); sweat rise then plateau (A1). (d) [2] Respiration releases heat (A1); production > loss (A1).

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "excretion".
items.answer: The removal from the body of waste products of metabolism, such as urea
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the removal from the body of waste products of metabolism, such as urea. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Why is urea produced rather than ammonia in mammals?
options: Urea is less toxic and can be stored and excreted in concentrated urine.
items.answer: Urea is less toxic and can be stored and excreted in concentrated urine.
items.markingKey: C. Toxicity.

items.stem: Explain the role of the loop of Henle.
items.answer: The ascending limb actively transports Na⁺ and Cl⁻ out into the medulla and is impermeable to water; the descending limb is permeable to water, which leaves by osmosis; countercurrent multiplier creates a high solute concentration deep in the medulla, allowing water to be reabsorbed from collecting ducts.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The ascending limb actively transports Na⁺ and Cl⁻ out into the medulla and is impermeable to water; the descending limb is permeable to water, which leaves by osmosis; countercurrent multiplier creates a high solute concentration deep in the medulla, allowing water to be reabsorbed from collecting ducts. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: In 24 hours a person’s kidneys filtered 551 g of sodium ions, and 5.4 g appeared in the urine. Calculate the percentage of the filtered sodium ions that was reabsorbed.
A person drinks 2 dm³ of water. Which change follows?
options: ADH secretion falls; fewer aquaporins; more dilute urine
items.answer: ADH secretion falls; fewer aquaporins; more dilute urine

items.stem: Explain the difference between ultrafiltration and selective reabsorption.
items.answer: Ultrafiltration is the non-selective, pressure-driven filtration of small molecules from blood into Bowman’s capsule; selective reabsorption is the return of useful substances from the filtrate to the blood by active transport, co-transport and osmosis.
items.markingKey: Ultrafiltration is the non-selective, pressure-driven filtration of small molecules from blood into Bowman’s capsule; selective reabsorption is the return of useful substances from the filtrate to the blood by active transport, co-transport and osmosis. items.stem: Kenji writes: "ADH makes more urine." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: ADH increases water reabsorption, so less, more concentrated urine is produced.
items.markingKey: ADH increases water reabsorption, so less, more concentrated urine is produced. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Why does ultrafiltration occur in the glomerulus?
options: The afferent arteriole is wider than the efferent arteriole, creating high blood pressure in the capillaries.
items.answer: The afferent arteriole is wider than the efferent arteriole, creating high blood pressure in the capillaries.
items.markingKey: C. Hydrostatic pressure.

items.stem: Briefly describe kidney dialysis and explain what it reveals about kidney function.
items.answer: Patients with kidney failure have blood passed through a dialyser with a partially permeable membrane and dialysis fluid. Dialysis fluid with normal concentrations of glucose and ions but no urea allows urea and excess ions to diffuse out, replacing filtration.
items.markingKey: Context (Patients with kidney failure have blood passed through a dialyser with a partially permeable membrane and dialysis fluid.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Which substance has the same concentration in plasma and glomerular filtrate?
items.answer: glucose
items.markingKey: D. Small solutes are freely filtered.

items.stem: Tomás writes: "Urea is made in the kidneys." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Urea is made in the liver from excess amino acids (deamination); kidneys excrete it.
items.markingKey: Urea is made in the liver from excess amino acids (deamination); kidneys excrete it. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the role of the kidney in excretion and osmoregulation, and compare dialysis with kidney transplant as treatments for kidney failure.
items.answer: Excretion of urea; osmoregulation by ADH; dialysis principle (diffusion across membrane, countercurrent, fluid composition); transplant benefits and risks.
items.markingKey: Excretion of urea; osmoregulation by ADH; dialysis principle (diffusion across membrane, countercurrent, fluid composition); transplant benefits and risks.

items.stem: "Kidney transplants are a better treatment for kidney failure than dialysis." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Transplants are generally better where a matched donor is available, while dialysis remains essential for those waiting or unsuitable.

items.answer: In the cold the hypothalamus secretes TRH, stimulating TSH from the anterior pituitary, which causes the thyroid to secrete thyroxine; thyroxine increases the metabolic rate of cells, so more heat is released by respiration.

items.stem: Explain how body temperature is regulated in humans.
items.answer: Set point 37 °C; thermoreceptors (skin, hypothalamus); hypothalamus as control centre; responses to heat: vasodilation, sweating, hair flattening; responses to cold: vasoconstriction, shivering, brown fat, thyroxine (TRH, TSH), hair erection; behaviour; negative feedback.
items.markingKey: Set point 37 °C; thermoreceptors (skin, hypothalamus); hypothalamus as control centre; responses to heat: vasodilation, sweating, hair flattening; responses to cold: vasoconstriction, shivering, brown fat, thyroxine (TRH, TSH), hair erection; behaviour; negative feedback.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "type 2 diabetes".
items.answer: A condition in which target cells become resistant to insulin, often linked to obesity and inactivity
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a condition in which target cells become resistant to insulin, often linked to obesity and inactivity. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Define the term "shivering".
items.answer: Rapid involuntary contraction of skeletal muscles that generates heat by respiration
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: rapid involuntary contraction of skeletal muscles that generates heat by respiration. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Where is glucose normally reabsorbed?
items.answer: the proximal convoluted tubule
items.markingKey: the proximal convoluted tubule. By co-transport with Na⁺.

items.stem: Explain the causes and treatment of type 1 and type 2 diabetes.
items.answer: Type 1: autoimmune destruction of β cells, little insulin; treated by insulin injections/pumps and monitoring; type 2: insulin resistance of target cells, linked to obesity, inactivity, genetics; treated by diet, exercise, weight loss and drugs such as metformin, later insulin.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Type 1: autoimmune destruction of β cells, little insulin; treated by insulin injections/pumps and monitoring; type 2: insulin resistance of target cells, linked to obesity, inactivity, genetics; treated by diet, exercise, weight loss and drugs such as metformin, later insulin. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "In vasodilation, blood vessels move closer to the skin surface." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Vessels do not move; arterioles widen so more blood flows through surface capillaries.
items.markingKey: Vessels do not move; arterioles widen so more blood flows through surface capillaries. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Why do the collecting ducts pass through the medulla?
options: The high solute concentration of the medulla draws water out of the ducts by osmosis.
items.answer: The high solute concentration of the medulla draws water out of the ducts by osmosis.
items.markingKey: C. Concentration gradient.

items.stem: Distinguish between glucagon and insulin.
items.answer: Insulin is secreted by β cells when glucose is high and lowers blood glucose by increasing uptake and glycogen synthesis; glucagon is secreted by α cells when glucose is low and raises blood glucose by stimulating glycogen breakdown.
items.markingKey: Insulin is secreted by β cells when glucose is high and lowers blood glucose by increasing uptake and glycogen synthesis; glucagon is secreted by α cells when glucose is low and raises blood glucose by stimulating glycogen breakdown. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Why does the body temperature of a person with fever stay high despite sweating stopping?
options: The hypothalamus set point has been raised, so the body maintains a higher temperature.
items.answer: The hypothalamus set point has been raised, so the body maintains a higher temperature.
items.markingKey: D. Altered set point.

items.stem: Explain how the structure of the glomerulus and Bowman’s capsule allows ultrafiltration.
items.answer: Afferent arteriole wider than efferent gives high hydrostatic pressure; fenestrated capillary endothelium; basement membrane acts as the filter, retaining proteins and cells; podocytes with filtration slits; water, glucose, urea, ions pass into the capsule.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Afferent arteriole wider than efferent gives high hydrostatic pressure; fenestrated capillary endothelium; basement membrane acts as the filter, retaining proteins and cells; podocytes with filtration slits; water, glucose, urea, ions pass into the capsule. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Fasting blood glucose of a patient with type 2 diabetes fell from 7.9 to 6.3 mmol dm⁻³ after six months of diet and exercise. Calculate the percentage change.
items.markingKey: (final − initial)/initial × 100 = (6.3 − 7.9)/7.9 × 100 (M1) = -20.3 % (A1); sign/direction required.

items.stem: A person in cold water stops shivering and becomes confused. What is happening?
options: Hypothermia: heat loss exceeds heat production and core temperature falls.
items.answer: Hypothermia: heat loss exceeds heat production and core temperature falls.
items.markingKey: D. Hypothermia.

items.stem:
The concentrations (g dm⁻³) of substances in plasma, glomerular filtrate and urine of a healthy person are shown. Filtrate is produced at 180 dm³ per day and urine at 1.4 dm³ per day.

Substance | Plasma | Filtrate | Urine
glucose | 1.03 | 1.03 | 0
amino acids | 0.47 | 0.47 | 0
urea | 0.32 | 0.32 | 20.5
sodium ions | 3.25 | 3.25 | 3.73
proteins | 76.0 | 0 | 0

(a) State which substance is present in plasma but not in filtrate. [1]
(b) Calculate the concentration factor of urea from plasma to urine. [1]
(c) Calculate the mass of urea filtered and the mass excreted per day, and the percentage reabsorbed. [3]
items.answer: (a) proteins (b) 64 (c) filtered 58 g; excreted 29 g; 50 % reabsorbed

items.stem: Blood glucose fell from 7.8 to 5.2 mmol dm⁻³ in 60 minutes. What was the mean rate of decrease?
items.answer: 0.043 mmol dm⁻³ min⁻¹

items.stem:
A student exercised on a cycle ergometer for 30 minutes in a warm room. Core (rectal) temperature, skin temperature and sweat rate were recorded.

Time / min | Core temperature / °C | Skin temperature / °C | Sweat rate / g h⁻¹
0 | 37.0 | 32.5 | 5
5 | 37.3 | 32.9 | 29
10 | 37.7 | 33.7 | 119
15 | 38.0 | 34.3 | 256
20 | 38.1 | 34.6 | 301
25 | 38.1 | 34.9 | 377
30 | 38.0 | 34.8 | 305

(a) State the maximum core temperature. [1]
(b) Calculate the heat lost per hour by evaporation at the final sweat rate (2.4 kJ g⁻¹), assuming all sweat evaporates. [1]
(c) Describe the changes in core temperature and sweat rate. [2]
items.answer: (a) 38.1 °C (b) 732 kJ h⁻¹ (c) Core temperature rises during the first 15–20 min then levels off; sweat rate rises sharply after a delay and then plateaus.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 38.1 (A1). (b) [1] 305 × 2.4 = 732 (A1). (c) [2] Core rise then plateau (A1); sweat rise then plateau (A1).

items.stem: A student claims: "The kidney filters only waste products from the blood." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: All small molecules are filtered, including useful ones, which are then reabsorbed.
items.markingKey: All small molecules are filtered, including useful ones, which are then reabsorbed. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

30 | 7.7 | 12.4
60 | 6.3 | 14.8
90 | 5.1 | 13.7
120 | 4.9 | 12.7
150 | 4.9 | 11.4

(a) State the maximum blood glucose of person B. [1]
(b) Calculate the mean rate of decrease in blood glucose of person A between 30 and 120 minutes. [2]
(c) Calculate the percentage increase in blood glucose of person B from 0 minutes to the maximum. [2]
items.answer: (a) 14.8 mmol dm⁻³ (b) 0.031 mmol dm⁻³ min⁻¹ (c) +94.7 %

items.stem: "Kidney transplants are a better treatment for kidney failure than dialysis." Discuss.
items.answer: Transplants are generally better where a matched donor is available, while dialysis remains essential for those waiting or unsuitable.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: restores near-normal kidney function and quality of life; cheaper in the long term. Arguments against: shortage of donors; long waiting lists; requires lifelong immunosuppressants with infection risk; rejection possible. Supported judgement: Transplants are generally better where a matched donor is available, while dialysis remains essential for those waiting or unsuitable. Markbands (7 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: "Endothermy is a better strategy than ectothermy." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Endothermy gives independence from environmental temperature at a high energy cost; which is better depends on habitat and food supply.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: endotherms can remain active in cold conditions and at night; enzymes work at a constant optimum. Arguments against: endotherms need much more food energy; ectotherms survive on less food and in deserts can be very successful. Supported judgement: Endothermy gives independence from environmental temperature at a high energy cost; which is better depends on habitat and food supply.
